nodes.name: Pulse electrodeposition of Ni-Cu without magnetic field
nodes.procedure: Pulse electrodeposition was performed with equal t_off and t_on for 160 s (the total electrodeposition time). E = 0 V and -1.1 V (vs. SCE) were applied during t_off and t_on, respectively. The electrodeposition was carried out using an electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, CHI630E, China) using a standard three-electrode cell with carbon paper (Toray, TGP-H-060, 0.19 mm in thickness, ca. 0.44 g cm^-3 in bulk density, and BET surface area 5.5 m^2 g^-1) with a square of 10 mm sides as exposed area as the working electrode (WE). Pt foil (10 mm × 10 mm × 0.5 mm) and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) were utilised as the counter electrode (CE) and the reference electrode (RE), respectively. All experimental equipment and electrodes were rinsed with deionised water (18 MΩ cm). The bath composition contained 0.05 M NiCl2·6H2O, 0.01 M CuCl2·2H2O, 0.05 M H3BO3, and 2.0 M NH4Cl. The pH of the electrolyte was adjusted to 3.0 ± 0.1 with the addition of dilute HCl, and the bath temperature was maintained at 35.0 ± 0.5 °C using a thermostat.

nodes.description: HER performance of Ni-Cu catalyst prepared without magnetic field (0 T) in 1 M KOH
nodes.source_text: Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed in 1 M KOH at a scan rate of 2 mV s⁻¹ with 95% iR-compensation to determine the HER activity. The 0 T sample exhibited the highest Ecorr with a value of -0.472 V (vs. SCE) and the highest icorr with a value of 7.011 × 10⁻⁵ A cm⁻². The overpotential at 10 mA cm⁻² was -89.6 mV and at 100 mA cm⁻² was -206.4 mV with a Tafel slope of 121.2 mV dec⁻¹.

nodes.description: HER performance of Ni-Cu catalyst prepared under 0.5 T perpendicular magnetic field in 1 M KOH
nodes.source_text: The 0.5 T ⊥ catalyst only needed overpotentials of -57.3 and -170.4 mV (vs. RHE) to deliver currents of 10 mA cm⁻² (η₁₀) and 100 mA cm⁻² (η₁₀₀), respectively. The Tafel slope was 99.4 mV dec⁻¹. To assess the electrochemical stability of 0.5 T ⊥ for the HER, chronoamperometry was conducted at a constant overpotential of -200 mV for 12 h. 0.5 T ⊥ showed negligible decrease of current density over a 12 h-HER test.

nodes.description: HER performance of Ni-Cu catalyst prepared under 0.5 T parallel magnetic field in 1 M KOH
nodes.source_text: The 0.5 T ∥ catalyst exhibited overpotentials of -59.3 and -181.9 mV (vs. RHE) at 10 mA cm⁻² and 100 mA cm⁻², respectively, with a Tafel slope of 106.8 mV dec⁻¹. The Ni–Cu catalysts made under the 0.5 T magnetic field showed better Ecorr and lower icorr with values of -0.254 V (vs. SCE) and 5.613 × 10⁻⁵ A cm⁻².
The 0.5 T ∥ catalyst exhibited overpotentials of -59.3 and -181.9 mV (vs. RHE) at 10 mA cm⁻² and 100 mA cm⁻², respectively, with a Tafel slope of 106.8 mV dec⁻¹.

nodes.description: HER performance of Ni-Cu catalyst prepared under 1.0 T perpendicular magnetic field in 1 M KOH
nodes.source_text: The poor performance of the 1.0 T ⊥ catalysts was mainly due to the excessive enhancement of the MHD effect. The Tafel slope was 148.7 mV dec⁻¹.

nodes.description: HER performance of Ni-Cu catalyst prepared under 1.0 T parallel magnetic field in 1 M KOH
nodes.source_text: The Tafel slope for 1.0 T ∥ was 123.3 mV dec⁻¹.

nodes.description: HER performance of Pt/C reference catalyst in 1 M KOH
nodes.source_text: A Pt/C (20 wt%) catalyst was also examined. It could be found that the Pt electrode had the best catalytic activity with a negligible overpotential to drive the HER. The Pt/C (20 wt%) catalyst showed the lowest Tafel slope (50.8 mV dec⁻¹).

nodes.description: EIS measurements of Ni-Cu catalysts at -290 mV vs. RHE in 1 M KOH
nodes.source_text: EIS measurements were performed over a frequency range from 10⁻¹ Hz to 10⁵ Hz with the amplitude of 10 mV on an electrochemical workstation (Bio-logic, VMP3, France). The 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥ attained smaller semicircles compared to 0 T, and the corresponding charge transfer resistances (Rct) for 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥ were only 2.097 and 3.39 Ω cm⁻². The Cdl values of 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥ were 1.68 and 1.32 times larger than that of 0 T.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM images show that without magnetic field (0 T), Ni–Cu deposits form large-scale dual-layer structures with spherical particles (325 nm) at the bottom and dendrite structures at the top on the single-sided plane of carbon paper. Under 0.5 T perpendicular magnetic field, dendrite structures are replaced by smaller uniformly distributed clusters (90 nm) surrounding the carbon paper. Under 0.5 T parallel magnetic field, similar uniformly distributed small-sized clusters (130 nm) are observed.
nodes.evidence_snippet: For the 0 T sample displayed in Fig. 6a, irregular and randomly distributed large-scale dual-layer structures grew on the single-sided plane of carbon paper ... the macro-MHD effect greatly eliminated the agglomeration, which replaced the dendrite structures with small-sized Ni–Cu clusters (90 nm).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS mapping of the 0.5 T perpendicular sample shows uniform distribution of Ni and Cu elements on the surface of the Ni–Cu deposit, indicating a homogenous coating on the carbon paper.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 6d is the EDS mapping of the 0.5 T ⊥ sample; the surface of the Ni–Cu deposit had a uniform distribution of Ni and Cu elements, indicative of a homogenous coating on the carbon paper.

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD patterns show that 0 T sample exhibits diffraction peaks indexed to Cu(111), Ni(111), Cu(200), Ni(200), and Ni(220) planes of face-centred cubic structure, confirming phase separation and two-phase Ni–Cu alloy formation. For 0.5 T perpendicular and 0.5 T parallel samples, only three peaks are detected with no Cu phases detected; Ni(111) plane positions shift toward smaller angles indicating Cu atoms incorporated into Ni lattice. The relative intensity of the (111) plane increases significantly under 0.5 T magnetic field.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The diffraction peaks for 0 T were indexed to Cu(111), Ni(111), Cu(200), Ni(200), and Ni(220) planes of the face-centred cubic (fcc) structure, respectively, confirming the phase separation and formation of the two-phase Ni–Cu alloy. For 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥, only three peaks were detected, no Cu phases were detected, and it was found that the positions of the Ni(111) plane ... shifted toward smaller angles ... the relative intensity of the (111) plane increased significantly under the 0.5 T magnetic field.

nodes.characterization_summary: Mean crystallite sizes calculated using the Scherrer equation show that Ni–Cu catalysts made under magnetic field have significantly reduced crystallite sizes compared to 0 T sample, with the perpendicular magnetic field producing the most refined crystallites.
nodes.evidence_snippet: From Fig. 8b, according to the Scherrer equation, for the Ni–Cu catalysts made under a magnetic field, the mean crystallite sizes were reduced significantly, which were refined by the magnetic field, especially the perpendicular magnetic field.

nodes.characterization_summary: Linear sweep voltammetry in 1 M KOH at 2 mV s⁻¹ scan rate with 95% iR-compensation shows that 0.5 T perpendicular Ni–Cu catalyst exhibits superior HER catalytic activity, requiring overpotentials of -57.3 mV at 10 mA cm⁻² and -170.4 mV at 100 mA cm⁻², approaching Pt/C catalyst performance. The 0.5 T parallel catalyst requires -59.3 mV and -181.9 mV respectively, while 0 T requires -89.6 mV and -206.4 mV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The 0.5 T ⊥ catalyst only needed overpotentials of -57.3 and -170.4 mV (vs. RHE) to deliver currents of 10 mA cm⁻² (η₁₀) and 100 mA cm⁻² (η₁₀₀), respectively.

nodes.characterization_summary: Tafel slopes derived from LSV curves show that 0.5 T perpendicular and 0.5 T parallel Ni–Cu catalysts have Tafel slopes of 99.4 and 106.8 mV dec⁻¹ respectively, significantly lower than 0 T (121.2 mV dec⁻¹), indicating better HER kinetics and lower overpotential requirement.
nodes.evidence_snippet: 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥ exhibited the Tafel slopes of 99.4 and 106.8 mV dec⁻¹, respectively, which were smaller than those of 0 T (121.2 mV dec⁻¹).

nodes.characterization_summary: Potentiodynamic polarization curves in 1 M KOH show that 0.5 T perpendicular and 0.5 T parallel catalysts have better corrosion potential (Ecorr = -0.247 V and -0.254 V vs. SCE respectively) and lower corrosion current density (5.435 × 10⁻⁵ and 5.613 × 10⁻⁵ A cm⁻² respectively) compared to 0 T (Ecorr = -0.472 V, icorr = 7.011 × 10⁻⁵ A cm⁻²), indicating better anti-corrosion performance and stability.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The 0 T sample exhibited the highest Ecorr with a value of -0.472 V (vs. SCE) and the highest icorr with a value of 7.011 × 10⁻⁵ A cm⁻². The Ni–Cu catalysts made under the 0.5 T magnetic field showed better Ecorr and lower icorr.

nodes.characterization_summary: Chronoamperometry conducted at constant overpotential of -200 mV for 12 hours shows that 0.5 T perpendicular Ni–Cu catalyst exhibits negligible decrease in current density, indicating favourable electrochemical stability for HER. SEM image after 12 h electrolysis shows morphology remains intact.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 9e, 0.5 T ⊥ showed negligible decrease of current density over a 12 h-HER test, which indicated favourable stability. In addition, the morphology of 0.5 T ⊥ still remained after the test (Fig. 9f).

nodes.characterization_summary: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy at -290 mV vs. RHE in 1 M KOH shows that 0.5 T perpendicular and 0.5 T parallel catalysts have significantly smaller charge transfer resistance (Rct = 2.097 and 3.39 Ω cm⁻² respectively) compared to 0 T (Rct = 8.959 Ω cm⁻²), indicating faster Faraday behaviour and lower contact resistance. Double-layer capacitance (Cdl) values for 0.5 T perpendicular and 0.5 T parallel are 1.68 and 1.32 times larger than 0 T respectively.
nodes.evidence_snippet: It was noticeable that 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥ attained smaller semicircles compared to 0 T, and the corresponding charge transfer resistances (Rct) for 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥ were only 2.097 and 3.39 Ω cm⁻². The Cdl values of 0.5 T ⊥ and 0.5 T ∥ were 1.68 and 1.32 times larger than that of 0 T.

nodes.characterization_summary: Cyclic voltammetry in Cu-only, Ni-only, and Ni–Cu baths at 35°C and 10 mV s⁻¹ scan rate shows two well-defined redox couples for Cu (Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ and Cu⁺/Cu⁰) and a single cathodic wave for Ni electrodeposition. In the binary Ni–Cu system, two reduction peaks at 1.0424 V and 0.5114 V are observed, attributed to Cu²⁺ to Cu⁺ and Cu⁺ to Cu⁰ reduction respectively, with co-deposition shifting peaks to lower overpotentials due to depolarisation effect.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The copper electrodeposition (Fig. 2c, 0.01 M CuCl₂·2H₂O) exhibited two well-defined redox couples (Cu²⁺/Cu⁺ and Cu⁺/Cu⁰), whereas for the nickel-containing electrolyte (Fig. 2b, 0.05 M NiCl₂·2H₂O), a single cathodic wave for electrodeposition of Ni was observed.

nodes.characterization_summary: Chronoamperometry applied to study nucleation and growth mechanism at different constant deposition potentials (-1.0 V, -1.1 V, -1.2 V vs. SCE) without magnetic field shows current-time transients characteristic of diffusion-limited nucleation with 3D nucleation and growth. At -1.1 V, sample initially follows instantaneous nucleation when t < tm but shifts toward progressive nucleation after tm, indicating secondary nucleation and dendritic structure formation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: From Fig. S2b (ESI†), it is worth noting that the sample made at -1.1 V initially followed instantaneous nucleation when t < tm, but shifted toward progressive nucleation after tm, which was evidence of secondary nucleation.

nodes.characterization_summary: Analysis using Scharifker-Hills model for diffusion-limited growth shows that nucleation mechanism changes from progressive nucleation under 0 T magnetic field to instantaneous nucleation under 0.5 T magnetic field throughout the entire electrodeposition process. The change is attributed to enhanced dispersion and increased density of nuclei induced by magnetohydrodynamic effect.
nodes.evidence_snippet: But with the superimposition of a 0.5 T magnetic field, the nucleation mechanism changed from progressive nucleation to instantaneous nucleation when t > tm. A similar current–time transient had been reported in the electrodeposition of Ni on a Au electrode, where the nucleation mechanism diverged to an instantaneous mechanism under a magnetic field.
